articles.title: Rochdale Cultural Organisations to Receive Share of £15 Million Funding
articles.excerpt: Cultural organisations in Rochdale will benefit from a £15 million funding package aimed at enhancing community engagement and wellbeing across Greater Manchester over the next three years.
articles.content_html:
Cultural organisations in Rochdale are set to benefit from a £15 million funding package announced by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA). This investment aims to enhance the impact of cultural initiatives on local communities and is part of Mayor Bev Craig's commitment to revitalise cultural engagement across the region.

The funding will be distributed over three years and will support various grassroots organisations, including music venues, community theatres, and production companies. The initiative focuses on promoting wellbeing, community cohesion, and cultural participation, particularly in areas such as youth engagement and disability arts.

Among the recipients is Breaking Barriers, a Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company that collaborates with local communities to amplify unheard voices. The organisation has been awarded £40,000 annually as part of the GMCA Culture Fund for the period 2026-2029. Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, expressed excitement about the funding, highlighting its significance in supporting community and cultural initiatives.

This funding is expected to foster a vibrant cultural landscape in Rochdale, providing opportunities for local residents to engage with the arts and participate in community-driven projects. The GMCA's investment reflects a broader strategy to restore pride in local areas and ensure that cultural activities are accessible to all.

Rochdale AFC manager Ian Watson has expressed satisfaction with the vast majority of his team's performance during the Jersey Mike’s Trophy tie against Liverpool Under-21s on Tuesday night. Watson noted that the players executed their game plan effectively, contributing to a strong showing against their opponents.

The match took place at the Crown Oil Arena, where Rochdale demonstrated their skills and teamwork throughout the game. Watson highlighted the importance of such fixtures for player development and team cohesion.

Looking ahead, Rochdale AFC will aim to maintain this momentum in their upcoming fixtures, with Watson likely to focus on further improving the team's performance as they progress in the tournament.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Invited to Join Great British Dog Walk for Hearing Dogs Charity
articles.excerpt: This October, residents of Rochdale can participate in the Great British Dog Walk, aiming to raise funds for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People while exploring local trails and landmarks.
articles.content_html:
Residents of Rochdale are encouraged to lace up their walking boots this October for the Great British Dog Walk, a charity initiative aimed at raising funds for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People. Participants are challenged to walk a total of 70 miles throughout the month, exploring the town’s scenic trails and historic landmarks while supporting a vital cause.

The campaign, supported by a puppy training hub located in Rochdale, invites walkers of all ages and abilities to take part. Each mile walked contributes to the training and support of hearing dogs, which can cost approximately £70,000 over their lifetime. This initiative not only promotes physical activity but also raises awareness about the impact of hearing dogs on the lives of deaf individuals.

Every step taken during the Great British Dog Walk carries significant meaning, as it directly contributes to the careful breeding, socialisation, and specialised training required to match these remarkable dogs with those who need them most. Participants can choose to explore new routes or add distance to their regular walks, making it a flexible and inclusive challenge.

To get involved, residents can register online and begin tracking their miles throughout October. This initiative not only supports a worthy cause but also encourages the community to engage with their local environment and discover hidden gems in Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale Draws 3-3 with Liverpool U21 in EFL Trophy Penalty Shootout
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC faced Liverpool Under-21s in a thrilling EFL Trophy match at Crown Oil Arena, ending in a dramatic penalty shootout after a 3-3 draw.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC hosted Liverpool Under-21s in a Northern Group H EFL Trophy match at Crown Oil Arena on September 22, 2026. The match concluded with a dramatic penalty shootout after both teams finished the game level at 3-3.

The game was a back-and-forth affair, with Rochdale initially taking the lead. However, Liverpool's young side fought back, showcasing their attacking prowess. The match was significant for both teams as they aimed for progression in the EFL Trophy, with Liverpool Academy currently sitting second in the group and Rochdale in third.

Rochdale's manager Ian Watson faced injury challenges, with several key players sidelined. Despite this, the team displayed resilience, having recently secured a 2-0 victory over Oldham Athletic in League Two. Liverpool U21s came into the match with confidence following a commanding 5-1 win against Brighton and Hove Albion Academy.

The penalty shootout saw Liverpool U21s emerge victorious, converting seven penalties to Rochdale's six. The match was officiated by referee Gareth Sheffield, who has experience officiating at Spotland. Fans were treated to a thrilling encounter, with both teams demonstrating their capabilities in a competitive atmosphere.

articles.title: Digital Autopsies to Reduce Invasive Post-Mortems in Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: The introduction of digital autopsies by the Coroner’s Office for Greater Manchester aims to reduce the need for invasive post-mortems by up to 80%, providing families with a less distressing option during their time of grief.
articles.content_html:
The Coroner’s Office for Greater Manchester has announced a pioneering initiative that could reduce the need for invasive post-mortems across Rochdale, Bury, and Oldham by up to 80%. This innovative service, developed in partnership with the NHS and specialist imaging providers Anubix and TIC Health, will utilise computed tomography (CT) scanning to help determine causes of death without the need for traditional invasive procedures.

The new digital autopsy service aims to alleviate the distress often caused to families during the grieving process. By employing post-mortem imaging, the coroner's office will assess whether a cause of death can be established without resorting to invasive methods, which can add to the emotional burden on relatives.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, expressed support for the initiative, stating that it addresses a highly sensitive issue and will enhance the coroner’s service. He noted that invasive post-mortems often cause additional anxiety for families, making this new service a timely and welcome development.

The coroner’s office plans to carry out several scans each week using this technology, with the long-term goal of expediting the process for families following the loss of a loved one. Joanne Kearsley, senior coroner for Manchester North, highlighted the importance of this advancement in providing better support to families during difficult times.

articles.title: Hopwood Hall College Launches Five-Year Strategy to Transform Lives Through Education
articles.excerpt: Hopwood Hall College has unveiled a new five-year strategy aimed at transforming lives and supporting local businesses and communities during an event at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Hopwood Hall College has launched an ambitious five-year strategy designed to enhance education and drive growth within the community. The unveiling took place during an event at Rochdale Town Hall, where Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE outlined the college's vision for the future, aiming to create new opportunities for individuals and businesses across the borough and beyond.

The event gathered students, staff, governors, employer partners, and community stakeholders, marking the beginning of an exciting chapter as the college prepares for its journey towards 2031. Hosted by Chris Maguire, executive editor of Business Cloud, the launch featured panel discussions that highlighted the positive impact of the college on its students and the local economy.

Among the speakers was Glory Frank, a former health and social care student who is now an ICU nurse. At 22 years old, she expressed her gratitude for the education she received at Hopwood Hall, stating that it significantly contributed to her professional development. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell also addressed attendees, emphasising the importance of the college in supporting the Rochdale community.

The college's strategy is expected to foster innovation and economic growth, positioning it as a leader in education and skills development. As the college embarks on this new initiative, it aims to strengthen its connections with local businesses and enhance the educational landscape for future generations.

articles.title: Who — or what — is the Healey Dwarf? Tracing the legend from Roby to the Heritage Centre
articles.excerpt: A guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure said to haunt Healey Dell, showing what the old printed collectors recorded, what later Victorian writers added, and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure said to haunt Healey Dell, showing what the old printed collectors recorded, what later Victorian writers added, and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Healey Dell is home to one of Rochdale borough’s most persistent pieces of local folklore: a small, bearded figure associated with the fairies and a feature known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The figure is usually called the Healey Dwarf in modern storytelling — a sentinel‑like stone or a tiny person who met the Fairy Queen — but the story we hear walking the Spodden today is the result of at least two centuries of retelling rather than a single documentary record.

The oldest readily available printed versions come from early nineteenth‑century folklore collecting. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published 1829–31) includes a long set of tales about Healey, “The Fairies’ Chapel” and the nearby cleft called the Thrutch; Roby’s chapters record the local romance‑style narratives then circulating and helped fix many of the plot elements later writers used. Roby’s work is a literary‑folklore source: it records what people were telling but is not a neutral archival record of events. For dating, Roby’s collections are the earliest printed witnesses I was able to locate. ([arc-codex.com](https://www.arc-codex.com/library/25256?utm_source=openai))

Later Victorian writers took up Roby’s materials and embellished them. A specifically titled book, Healey Dell, or The History [in Verse] of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, appeared in 1882 (R. Standring). Standring’s work is a clearly literary and romantic reworking: it gives a full narrative about a character called Healey (described in jaunty costume with a ginger beard) being offered a place among the fairies and taking the form of a stone guardian in the river. That 1882 text is an important source for how the dwarf appears in later local guidebooks and family storytelling. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Healey_Dell_Or_The_History_in_Verse_of_F.html?id=IYMNAAAAYAAJ&utm_source=openai))

How the story sits with the place you can visit today is straightforward to separate. Healey Dell is a documented nature reserve and visitor attraction with industrial archaeology (old mills and a prominent Victorian viaduct) and a heritage centre that interprets the site for visitors. The borough’s directory entry and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre both explain the real, physical origin of the Fairies’ Chapel name: the River Spodden has carved a niche in the rock (a pulpit‑like alcove and seats) that easily invited imaginative readings as a tiny “chapel” of the fairies, and Victorian tourists specialised in that kind of romantic topography. Those facts about the reserve and its facilities are supported by Rochdale Borough Council’s site listing and the heritage centre’s material. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale?utm_source=openai))

Modern retellings at the heritage centre and in local guides often weave Roby and Standring together, and sometimes add Victorian‑era motifs (a prophetic Fairy Queen; witches turned to stone; prophetic local fortunes). The centre openly treats these stories as legend and performs them for visitors — for example, the site’s guide materials and a short printed “Fairies’ Chapel” guide present the Healey Dwarf story as part of the Dell’s folklore rather than as a historical event. Erosive geology and historic floods are cited to explain why the rock shapes and river features described by nineteenth‑century writers may not look identical now. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf?utm_source=openai))

What we can say with confidence, and what we should treat as folklore: facts — the place, the rock niche, the industrial remains, the viaduct and the existence today of a heritage centre and nature reserve — are verifiable; the Healey Dwarf as a supernatural person or as a stone sentinel with fairy agency is a narrative motif preserved in nineteenth‑century collections and in later local retellings. Roby (1829–31) and Standring (1882) are the best early printed witnesses of the tale; later accounts draw on them and on the Dell’s Victorian reputation as a beauty spot. If a claim cannot be found in archival records or contemporary documentary sources (for example, a dated eyewitness affidavit or an official inspection reporting “a dwarf”), it should be treated plainly as folklore and local tradition rather than as documented fact. ([arc-codex.com](https://www.arc-codex.com/library/25256?utm_source=openai))

If you go looking for the Healey Dwarf today, bring an appetite for both geology and story. Stand by the Thrutch and you’ll see the water‑carved niche that inspired the “Fairies’ Chapel” name; follow the heritage centre’s displays for the Victorian and folkloric layers of the tale; and read Roby if you want the earliest printed atmosphere of the story that fixed many of the characters and episodes. Where Roby and Standring record what people told in the nineteenth century, the modern council and heritage‑centre material remind visitors we are dealing with cultural memory and storytelling as much as with stones and riverbeds. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale?utm_source=openai))

articles.title: Ben White Joins Rochdale Hornets as New Halfback
articles.excerpt: Ben White has signed with Rochdale Hornets after leaving Batley Bulldogs, aiming to strengthen the team for the upcoming season.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets have announced the signing of halfback Ben White, who joins the club following a seven-season spell with Batley Bulldogs. The 31-year-old, a product of the Leeds Rhinos academy, is expected to bring valuable experience to the team as they aim to improve on their 15th-place finish in the Championship last season.

Chairman Andy Mazey expressed enthusiasm for the signing, describing White as a significant addition to the squad. He noted that White's experience, which includes representing Germany at the international level and playing for clubs such as Swinton Lions and Halifax Panthers, makes him a suitable fit for the Hornets.

White will be working alongside Jamie Dallimore, with whom he has previously collaborated at Barrow Raiders. The Hornets are keen to build a competitive squad under the guidance of coach Gary Thornton, especially after losing Jack Hansen to Widnes Vikings.

The club is hopeful that White's addition will help them climb the Championship table in the upcoming season, as they continue to strengthen their roster ahead of the new campaign.

articles.title: Middleton Residents Campaign to Preserve Kickpitch Amid Plans for Car Park
articles.excerpt: Residents of the Langley Estate in Middleton are actively campaigning to retain their community kickpitch, which is set to be replaced by a car park for the Burnside Centre.
articles.content_html:
Residents in the Langley Estate of Middleton are campaigning to keep their community kickpitch, which is slated for removal to make way for a car park. The pitch, located on Burnside Crescent next to the Burnside Centre, serves as a vital hub for local sports and community activities.

The decision to decommission the pitch comes as part of plans to create a car park for the Burnside Centre. Families have expressed concerns, stating that the pitch is an essential space for children and young people to engage in football and other sports. The pitch is one of three on the estate, and campaigners are advocating for a new facility to be built on adjacent land rather than losing the existing one.

Residents have been informed that replacement facilities will be available at Rochdale AFC and the planned Football and Community Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee Playing Fields. However, many feel that these alternatives do not adequately replace the local access and community spirit fostered by the existing kickpitch.

The Burnside Centre has acknowledged the community's disappointment, citing concerns over antisocial behaviour and the pitch's deteriorating condition as reasons for the decision. The centre noted that the pitch, established in the late 1990s, had reached the end of its expected lifespan and required significant investment to remain operational. Local resident Kelly Burton, a mother of four, emphasised the importance of the pitch as a safe space for children to meet and play together.

articles.title: Peacocks Clothing Store Signs Long-Term Lease at Rochdale Riverside
articles.excerpt: RivingtonHark has secured a long-term lease for Peacocks at Rochdale Riverside, increasing the shopping centre's occupancy to 92%.
articles.content_html:
RivingtonHark has announced that Peacocks, a well-known clothing retailer, has signed a long-term lease for a 10,181 sq ft unit at Rochdale Riverside. This development brings the shopping centre's occupancy rate to 92%, reflecting strong demand for retail space in the area.

The Rochdale Riverside complex, which spans 200,000 sq ft, has seen a significant increase in footfall, with a reported 15.3% rise year-on-year. In July alone, nearly 200,000 visitors frequented the centre. Since its opening in 2020, Rochdale Riverside has been managed by RivingtonHark, which has been working with Rochdale Council to enhance the retail offering.

Ollie Holland, asset manager for Rochdale Riverside at RivingtonHark, stated that the addition of Peacocks strengthens the diverse fashion options available at the centre. He noted that this letting demonstrates continued confidence from national retailers in the long-term appeal of Rochdale Riverside.

As the centre approaches full occupancy, further lettings are anticipated, which could enhance the shopping experience for local residents and visitors alike. The presence of national brands like Peacocks, alongside existing retailers such as M&S, H&M, and JD Sports, is expected to contribute positively to the local economy.

articles.title: Inquest Finds Drink-Driving Contributed to Heywood Man's Fatal Crash
articles.excerpt: An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place in Rochdale on July 1, 2024.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

02:03, 23 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into a pub in Heywood.

An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place after crashing into a pub in Heywood.

An inquest has determined that Will Place, 23, died after crashing his car into a pub in Heywood while over the drink-drive limit following a football match.

23:21, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into a pub in Heywood, following a night of drinking after an England football match.

23:09, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into the White Lion pub in Heywood.

21:30, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing in the fatal crash of 23-year-old Will Place, which occurred during a high-speed pursuit in Rochdale on July 1, 2024.

An inquest jury has determined that Greater Manchester Police officers acted appropriately during a high-speed pursuit that ended in the fatal crash of 23-year-old Will Place in Rochdale on July 1, 2024. The incident occurred after Place, who had been drinking, ran a red light in front of a marked police van, prompting officers to initiate a chase.

The pursuit began at approximately 3:00 a.m. after Place left a local venue where he had watched an England soccer match. Officers reported that the vehicle reached speeds of up to 70 mph in 30 mph zones. However, police control instructed officers to discontinue the chase shortly after it began due to a lack of tactical pursuit resources. Despite this, Place lost control of his vehicle and crashed into the White Lion pub at the junction of Rochdale Road and York Street, resulting in a fire and partial building collapse.

During the inquest at Rochdale Coroner's Court, PC Sarah Hardman, who was driving the pursuing police van, explained that she activated her emergency lights and sirens after witnessing Place's reckless driving. She stated that the decision to pursue was proportionate at the time, and she believed it was her duty to attempt to stop the vehicle to prevent further danger. The chase was called off before the crash occurred, and she did not activate her body-worn camera as her focus was on driving safely.

The inquest also revealed that toxicology tests indicated Place's blood alcohol level was 163mg per decilitre, which is more than double the legal limit. Family members expressed their grief over his loss, with his mother, Beverley Place, describing him as a loving and thoughtful young man who had a promising future ahead of him.

articles.title: Ex-Prisoner Jamie Dale Advocates for Support in Early Release Scheme
articles.excerpt: Jamie Dale, a former prisoner from Rochdale, emphasises the need for support from ex-offenders in government plans for early inmate release to prevent reoffending and homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Jamie Dale, a former prisoner from Rochdale, has voiced concerns regarding the government's plans to release inmates early as a measure to alleviate prison overcrowding. Dale, who spent over 11 years in prison for his involvement in organised crime, now runs the Old Lags Network, a support initiative aimed at helping ex-offenders reintegrate into society.

Dale argues that the success of such early release schemes hinges on the involvement of individuals who have experienced the prison system firsthand. He believes that without adequate support, many released prisoners may struggle to adjust, leading to a high rate of reoffending. "Most of the people who return quite quickly have not got great family networks," he stated.

The Old Lags Network, established in September 2025, focuses on bridging the gap between prison and community, aiming to reduce the number of individuals who fall through the cracks after their release. Dale emphasised that many ex-offenders end up homeless, which exacerbates the cycle of reoffending. He believes that including ex-prisoners in the development of support solutions could significantly decrease the number of individuals recalled to prison.

As the government continues to explore early release options, Dale's insights highlight the critical need for comprehensive support systems that address the challenges faced by former inmates. His advocacy underscores the importance of community involvement in creating effective rehabilitation pathways.

articles.title: Inquest Jury Clears Police Following Fatal High-Speed Chase in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: An inquest jury has found no wrongdoing by Greater Manchester Police in a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place, who crashed into a pub in Heywood.
articles.content_html:
An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that ended in the fatal crash of 23-year-old Will Place. The incident occurred on July 1, 2024, when Place's vehicle collided with the White Lion pub at the junction of Rochdale Road and York Street in Heywood.

The pursuit began around 3:00 a.m. after Place, who had been drinking following an England soccer match, ran a red light in front of a marked police van. Officers activated their emergency lights and pursued him, reporting speeds of up to 70 mph in 30 mph zones. However, police control instructed officers to discontinue the chase shortly after, due to a lack of tactical pursuit resources. Despite this, Place lost control of his vehicle and crashed into the pub shortly thereafter, suffering fatal injuries.

During the inquest at Rochdale Coroner's Court, PC Sarah Hardman, the officer driving the pursuing police van, explained the operational decisions made during the chase. She stated that the pursuit was deemed necessary at the time to prevent further reckless driving, but was called off before the crash occurred. Toxicology tests later revealed that Place's blood alcohol level was more than double the legal limit, contributing to the circumstances of the incident.

Family members of Will Place expressed their grief during the inquest, highlighting his character and the impact of his loss. His mother, Beverley Place, described him as a loving and kind young man with a promising future, having recently graduated in sports journalism.

articles.title: Why does Rochdale say ‘cruckle’?
articles.excerpt: A short look at a small local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means in Rochdale, where it comes from and why linguists find it interesting.
articles.summary: A short look at a small local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means in Rochdale, where it comes from and why linguists find it interesting.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” (also heard as “cruckled”) is used to mean rolling or twisting one’s ankle — the awkward half‑stumble you can often walk off but which still makes you wince. This sense turns up repeatedly in folk descriptions of Rochdale speech and in the Manchester area project work that asked residents to name words they associate with each borough. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

The word’s association with Rochdale is not just anecdote. A 2024 perceptual‑dialectology study of Greater Manchester (the “draw‑a‑map / keywords” method) collected 349 participants’ comments about local accents and vocabulary; in the dataset “cruckle” (spelt there as “cruckle”/“cruckled”) appears among words respondents list for Rochdale alongside other locally salient items such as “guinnel” (ginnel). That academic study — published in the Journal of Linguistic Geography — presents the word as part of residents’ folk‑linguistic map of the borough. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

But ‘cruckle’ is not an accidental modern invention. Historical dialect lexicography records older relatives of the form — crookle, crunkle, crankle and similar spellings — with meanings in the same semantic field: to bend, make crooked, crumple, stoop or hobble. Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that fit those older meanings; other historical glossaries and etymological work link crook‑/crunk‑ roots to words for bending and rumpling. In Scots dialect lexicons the cognate crunkle has long been attested with senses like “to crumple” or “to make a rustling/crackling sound.” These sources show that the form family is old and regional rather than a brand‑new local coinage. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

So why does Rochdale use it to mean twisting an ankle? Part of the answer is semantic extension and local persistence. Roots meaning “bend” or “crumple” naturally extend to bodily movement — stooping, limping, or twisting a limb — and the frequentative/agentive endings that appear in dialect verbs (‑le, ‑le‑type forms) are common in northern English and Scots. Over generations a local pronunciation and narrow semantic focus (here, an ankle‑roll) can become the everyday sense people use and recognise. Linguists therefore see Rochdale’s “cruckle” as a local survival and narrowing of a wider, older dialect verb group rather than a wholly unique word created in isolation. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is ‘cruckle’ unique to Rochdale? That depends on how you count uniqueness. Perceptual and folk‑linguistic evidence show Rochdale residents and many Greater Manchester respondents strongly associate the word with the borough; that social recognition is an important part of the word’s identity. At the same time, historical records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots: dialect words seldom obey modern administrative borders. In short, the root is regional but the living habit and local pride in “I cruckled” feel especially Rochdale. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

Why do dialect researchers pay attention to small words like this? Because they do two jobs at once: they reveal how people actually speak now and they show how non‑linguists think about place and identity. Words such as “cruckle” become data points for change, contact (for example Lancashire–Yorkshire effects across town boundaries), and social meaning — little markers people use to signal where they are from. Projects that combine historical dictionaries with contemporary perceptual mapping give a fuller picture: an old verb family survives in a recognisably local form, and that form is part of how Rochdalians hear and describe themselves. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

If you don’t know the word, try it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll likely get a nod of recognition from someone from round here. If you want to follow up, the perceptual study (Dann et al., Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024) and the older dialect dictionaries are good starting points: one gives contemporary social mapping, the others give the historical spread and senses that help explain how the Rochdale meaning developed. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

articles.title: Mark Street Roadworks Scheduled for 24 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Roadworks on Mark Street in Rochdale will result in a temporary closure from midnight to 11.59pm on Saturday, 24 October 2026, affecting traffic flow in the area.
articles.content_html:
Mark Street in Rochdale will be temporarily closed on Saturday, 24 October 2026, from midnight until 11.59pm. The closure will affect the section of Mark Street between its junctions with Halifax Road and Athol Street.

During this period, no waiting will be permitted in the affected area. Motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly, as the closure may impact traffic flow on nearby roads, including Halifax Road, Davyhulme Street, and Athol Street.

This roadwork is part of ongoing maintenance efforts by Rochdale Borough Council to improve local infrastructure. Residents and commuters are encouraged to check the Rochdale Borough Council website for updates on the roadworks and any further announcements regarding local traffic changes.

For more information, including a map of the roadworks, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. The council also provides a map of roadworks across Greater Manchester for those needing to navigate around the closures.

In 1871 The Black Dyke Band performed at the original opening ceremony for Rochdale Town Hall. Since the post refurbishment of the Town Hall, the band have since gone on to perform every year bringing the best of brass band quality for all to enjoy. Join them again in 2027.
